utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kaiser. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kaiser. Mr. Kaiser, do you remember a meeting you had in Zagreb with the deputy minister of the Republic of Croatia for culture whose name was Prosper Nowak, if memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this meeting, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that that meeting he referred to an initiative by the citizens of Dubrovnik to internationalise the Dubrovnik problem at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was concern about what the -- I think what the local authorities of Dubrovnik were doing in their various discussions with the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about this. What was this concern about? What was it that the local authorities were doing in their negotiations with the federal authorities that caused concern to the central authorities in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult to say because they never really explained to us what the local authorities in Dubrovnik might, in fact, be doing. There was genuine concern about the discussions. I don't know if this was a -- as you know, I mean Dubrovnik has had a long history of autonomy and Dubrovnikers and the Dalmations in -- generally have a reputation of being rather different from the rest of the Croats. I don't know the exact basis of the fears that they had. This internationalisation discussion, of course, also went part and parcel in fact with what Dubrovnik was doing -- not Dubrovnik but what UNESCO was doing, running up the flags and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that there was an initiative on the part of the local authorities in Dubrovnik that was opposed to Zagreb's policies at the time, the official policies?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears that there was such a suspicion, at least on the part of the authorities of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your impression that the authorities in Zagreb were trying to suppress any such initiative?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authorities in Zagreb were really going through a lot of panicking. I think this is a -- this is something that struck us very, very much. I believe Vukovar had just fallen. There was a lot of fear. And this fear probably involved different aspects of different things going on, in fact, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I can't really put my finger exactly on what the fear would have been. I think it certainly was some -- I suspect that there was some sort of autonomy being negotiated. This is I think what it was about, but I don't know exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps ever hear about an initiative that proposed the de-militarisation of Dubrovnik and for Dubrovnik to be placed under international control as a means of avoiding conflict that was beginning to break out at the time? Was all of this perhaps a reference to such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing exactly this discussion about turning it into kind of an UN protectorate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not make myself sufficiently clear. I did not mean in terms of protectorate. I meant for Dubrovnik to be placed under any kind of protection by the international community in view of the historical significance of the general Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean the point of view -- the mission of UNESCO in the framework of The Hague convention and also the World Heritage Convention, the gesture of running up the UN flags over the walls of the Old Town of Dubrovnik was clearly an attempt on the part of UNESCO to try to preserve this town from whatever military action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zagreb did you get the impression that the authorities in Zagreb were trying to suppress this initiative that you were not exactly clear about but that was at any rate in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a question of trying to put an assistant minister on a boat. And you might regard that as an attempt to suppress something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may just read out a sentence from your statement, which reads: "Prosper Nowak said that he wanted to go with us, the reference is to Dubrovnik, to check on what Dubrovnik people were doing and to ensure that we did not internationalise Dubrovnik. He explained he wanted the town to remain under the Croatian authorities and part of Croatian sovereignty." Did I quote you correctly and what did you think that meant?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. I mean, you've quoted me correctly. The internationalisation of the town would I suppose go somewhere to ensuring some sort of autonomy, which was what I suppose that the authorities in Zagreb were afraid of would take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were taking steps to prevent that from happening. You, yourself, witnessed one of those measures that were being taken, and perhaps there were other such measures being taken at the time. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the other measures were, but there certainly was an attempt to put Mr. Nowak on the vessel which we were going to take to go to Dubrovnik. And perhaps Mr. Nowak thought that he could go down and by himself suppress autonomous activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's as much as you know. But perhaps there was something else happening at the time. Would you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that question. That's inviting speculation. The witness has given his --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to another meeting that you had in Zagreb with a JNA officer whose name was Stamenkovic. Can you please tell me where exactly you met this man, under what circumstances, and when, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we met him very briefly because he actually came to the headquarters of the ECMM in the hotel. That was brief. And then when we had a longer meeting with him, it was -- it was the command building of the 5th Military District in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this building was? Is it in the centre of town? Do you remember anything about of the location of the building?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- it was a central location, if I remember properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have trouble reaching the building on your way to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Croatian military around the headquarters of the 5th Military District towards the end of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what made the atmosphere in Zagreb very strange. You didn't see any Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that soldiers and officers from the 5th Military District HQ were free to move about Zagreb in late November 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't imagine they had so much freedom to move around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me why.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way: Zagreb was in a -- if you will permit me just to make a few comments about the -- sort of the environment or the ambience of Zagreb when we came there. Zagreb was in a very strange state of mind and condition. I mean, it's the type of place where in the morning you can see all the rush-hour traffic, great big traffic jams, people coming in to go to work. And at night there was shooting. We were in an Intercontinental Hotel which was a great big hotel, a splendid restaurant, but every morning there would be 600 refugees in the lobby. The top two storeys of the hotel were, you know, were condemned. You couldn't use them, I suppose, perhaps because -- for fear of air raids. There were people wandering around -- strange people wandering around the hotel. And I remember one occasion there was a chap with his gun out walking down the corridors. If you consider that this was a very, very strange setting and an unreliable one, and if there was shooting at night I would find it very hard to imagine -- there was also what they call the "police hour". I find it very hard to imagine that people could move around very easily, especially if they are wearing a uniform. It was not appreciated in the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not hear that the JNA barracks in Zagreb had been blocked at the time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- now that you mention it, yes, because I had heard that many, many of the barracks buildings of the JNA throughout Croatia, in fact, were blockaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night shooting that you have referred to, these were probably shootouts between the JNA soldiers on the one hand and the Croat military surrounding the barracks in which the JNA forces were still stationed, wasn't it? Or you simply don't know. If so, please just let us move on.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This officer you met, Stamenkovic, did he say anything about the mortars surrounding the Old Town rampart in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of a meeting at the 5th Military District, one of the officers did in fact say that -- made an allusion to the mortars. What I remember is this was the -- sort of the second allusion to the mortars. I can't remember for sure if it was Stamenkovic or if it was perhaps General Raseta himself. Because at the end of one of the meeting Raseta came in and we had a short conversation with him, but it was said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that General Raseta was the commander of the 5th Military District?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the 5th Military District.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that at the 5th Military District HQ they were all familiar with the situation in and around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very honest, it's very hard to say. I think maybe it was very far away for them. There was no -- there was not much in the way of details. It was a very vague, sort of general discussion. It was probably along the lines of earlier discussions that we had had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zagreb, did you meet any representatives of the European Community mission in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who precisely did you meet?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember meeting Ton Kampenars [phoen] who was a monitor who I met on a number of occasions later on in the Croatian-Bosnian wars because he worked there for a while. I can't remember the names of the other gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps meet any of those monitors who were in the former Yugoslavia at the time these days in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did meet a chap who in fact had been at Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to talk to him?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we talked mainly about his horses and his dogs because I'm not supposed to talk to him about anything referring to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He made no reference at all to his testimony, I assume?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that man back in Dubrovnik at the time when he was there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw him, I vaguely remembered him. The years have gone on. We both have gotten older. We didn't have very much contact with him obviously, but I vaguely remember this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact at all with the monitors in Dubrovnik, especially in those days, the 4th, the 5th, and the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any contact with them about -- around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you sort of vaguely remembered him? Was it from Zagreb or from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there -- I just vaguely remember somebody, sir. There -- there weren't so many internationals in the town. I think what you might expect -- a few of them you might actually remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remember anyone else you saw in Dubrovnik when you were there in late November and early December, any other monitor specifically?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any monitors specifically. I couldn't describe them to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to briefly go back to General Raseta. Do you remember what he said? Did you know what his views were on what you talked about, the reason you went to see him at the 5th Military District HQ, I mean?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's normal that we would try to see the top-most officer. As I said, most of discussions with lieutenant -- or Colonel Stamenkovic -- Raseta was -- came in, he was extremely -- he was very, very polite. He -- there was not much -- not really so much of a discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps use the opportunity to convey to the commander of the 5th Military District your concern about the bombardment of Dubrovnik in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned earlier that we didn't talk very much about these bombardments or these mortars at the foots of walls and things like that. I mean, when we -- it wasn't necessary to -- I mean, everybody knew why we were going to Dubrovnik. Everybody knew what had been alleged, so there was no particular point in lecturing anybody or speculating on this or speculating on that. I mean, this is just not the way it was done. It may sound strange, but in fact that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last Friday you told us that when in Belgrade you turned down the proposal of the federal -- of the federal authorities for federal experts to join you on your way to Dubrovnik. However, both you and your colleague from the mission accepted that a Croatian assistant minister should join you. Can you please explain how it was that your colleague and yourself made the decision to bring the Croatian deputy minister along while you had turned down the proposal for the federal experts to join you. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- I've already explained the -- sort of the general atmosphere in Zagreb. It was kind of a feeling of impending doom that hung over everybody's head. The most unpleasant meeting that we had, in fact, before we arrived in Dubrovnik was in fact that first meeting with the Croatian officials. It was very, very unpleasant. There was a lot of tension in the air, and there was a lot of tension about which boat we were going to take and which direction we were going to come from. You yourself have alluded to some statements made by Mr. Nowak about the danger of if we come in on a federal boat, provoking the people of Dubrovnik, and this statement was in fact said twice. And it was quite clear that this was not just an information statement about a few people throwing tomatoes or perhaps even spitting on somebody. The fact that it was underlined in the context of annoyance. We were told that UNESCO didn't care where Dubrovnik was, which country it was in. There were -- things that were like that said, quite aggressive. And the question was: Well, how are we going to get to Dubrovnik under those circumstances? And you could say this was sort of a tactical concession in order for us to carry out our mission, that is to actually to get to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you then set out with this assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did set out -- we set out with him from Zagreb to Rijeka and we got to Rijeka with him. However, there's another element into -- into the story -- is that, you will remember that there was -- Mr. Janicot had returned to Paris. And Mr. Vogric was with us in Zagreb, and Mr. Vogric had also returned to Paris in order to brief Mr. Janicot about the progress of the mission. So we got as far as Rijeka with Mr. Nowak and then we entered into conversation, into discussion with Mr. Janicot who had been completely briefed by Mr. Vogric on our confession [sic]. And of course Mr. Janicot was quite angry about this and we were recalled to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was Mr. Janicot angry?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Janicot was angry because Mr. Janicot was a very -- was a very, very talented N-ARC [phoen], he was a very talented UNESCO functionary. He was a director of the cabinet, director-general. And of course he realised that you simply can't go around improvising your trips and improvising who you're going with and which routes you going to take and that sort of a thing. And it certainly seemed that it would not be a very good idea diplomatically in order to actually go on the boat to Dubrovnik with an assistant minister of culture. It would not help the credibility of our organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously you disagreed with that, given the fact that you had set out from Zagreb in the company of the same assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mission, as I understood it and as we understood it, was that we did have to get to Dubrovnik. It was very important for the representatives of UNESCO, the observer mission, to get there. So we were going there. At the same time, we knew that Mr. Vogric would be going back to Paris and that Mr. Vogric was inform Mr. Janicot of the decision we had made, that is the concession -- the improvisation in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore it seems that the Croatian authorities had exerted a great deal of pressure on you, even if you choose to euphemistically refer to it as a tactical concession. Am I correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pressure, it was a great deal of pressure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yield to that pressure?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we -- of course we yielded to it. We yield led because we got on the same vehicle with Mr. Nowak and we went to Rijeka at the same time as Mr. Vogric was going back to Paris.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you give in to this pressure, contrary to the policy of the institution that you worked for to accompany one of the sides in the conflict to accomplish your mission, while at the same time refusing to go on that same mission with the other side in the conflict? Wasn't that so?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I only really discovered the arts of diplomacy a little bit especially working in Bosnia-Herzegovina when one has to deal with three different sides. This was a mistake on our part. It -- I understand perfectly Mr. Janicot's reaction, but as I said I wasn't too surprised at his reaction really. At the same time we were trying to keep open all the different options. It was very, very important to get to Dubrovnik. Not to go to Dubrovnik, I think, would not have been a good thing either for Dubrovnik or, let's say, the commitments of the United Nations and it certainly wouldn't have been a good thing for UNESCO. But if it had been the only option open, it would have been a disastrous mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this heavy pressure existed while you were in Zagreb and even heavier pressure when you arrived in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there is much -- actually, there is much more pressure from authorities in Zagreb who themselves were very far away from Dubrovnik and wondering what was going on and possibly inventing things that were going on. In Dubrovnik there was not at all that kind of pressure. The aggressiveness which we felt in the meeting with Nowak and his colleagues and also we felt at other moments in the Croatian press. I mean, extremely nasty, nasty articles about us running the flag up over Dubrovnik and taking it away, taking down the Croatian flag, taking Dubrovnik away. I remember a really nasty encounter I had with a journalist who saw me with the keys to the walls and said: Only UNESCO has the keys to the walls. UNESCO won't let any Croat up on the walls of Dubrovnik, which was a lot of nonsense. Any people could go up, but people didn't want to go up. I mean, the pressures in Dubrovnik, they were -- there were no pressures compared to what we felt in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any problems in Dubrovnik with the Croatian armed forces in Dubrovnik which were under the direct control of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any dealings with the armed forces, but we didn't have any problems with them either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This media pressure which existed there exerted on you and your activities, did it influence the attitude that you adopted, vis-a-vis the problems that you had to grapple with, or were you in blockaded Dubrovnik completely immune to such pressures?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident with the keys, I think it happened after the 6th of December. And I can't remember the exact printing of -- the date of the printing of the particular article which we saw in the Zagreb press. But there was really -- if there was a pressure, as I said, it was an extraneous pressure. It came from Zagreb, whether it was in Zagreb with the ministers or whether it was the medias of Zagreb that showed up down in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the impression there -- was Zagreb actually in control of the authorities of -- in Dubrovnik and the armed forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I really can't answer that, because these are the types of questions that sort of went -- they went beyond my particular part of the mission. What I did pick up was not from politicians, but it was often from people, little people, who felt that they were abandoned. It's not a question under the pressure of Zagreb, but they felt that they were abandoned by Zagreb. And they were always complaining about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain in briefly what detail -- I do not wish to dwell on this. Just by way of detail when you sailed into the port of Zelenika. You said Serbian policemen stopped you and said this or that. What do you mean when you refer to Serbian policemen in Zelenika, or Serbian police? What Serbian police in Zelenika are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry this is Serbian used in a generic way. It would be some sort of emanation, either local authorities or federal authorities. I don't know exactly what units these people were from. I got the feeling that they were police and I thought there also may have been customs -- customs officers among them. But whether Montenegrin, whether Serbian, whether federal, whether republic, whether municipal, whether military, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but for you these were Serbian policemen. This is how you experienced them or you expected to come across a Serbian policeman there, at least that is what you said to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I said they were Serbian policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first day of your stay in Dubrovnik you say that you and your colleague Carnez went around the streets collecting shrapnel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did go around the streets collecting shrapnel. We began to look at the damage that we saw, and unfortunately I pulled out one of these cylinders from the house in Ulica Boskoviceva. There was one moment when we went up the walls to Minceta when I found little fragments, which I think were shrapnel, and that I actually did collect and put it in my hand. But I -- we weren't going around collecting shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the shrapnel where you found it or did you take it with you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, these very small pieces which I picked up on the wall, I took it with me. The -- if you're -- when you say "shrapnel," if you're talking about -- we weren't so interested in shrapnel, but if there was a piece of something, we didn't take it with us. We just noted down that there had been this piece. You have to keep in mind as well, sir, that the people kept the fragments that -- the tail cylinders, the tails of mortars, they actually kept them and we didn't ask them to give them to us. We just noted down and sometimes we photographed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know on that day what it was that you found? How did you know that it was shrapnel, that it was something that was part of a shell?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I'm not a military expert and I don't claim to be a military expert. The cylinders which I pulled out, or the tails of mortars -- well, we've sort of seen the drawings of these things. I mean, I assumed that that's what they were because those are military things. I don't know what else they could be except tails of mortars or tails of projectiles. The -- if you're talking about how would one identify smaller pieces of shrapnel --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm asking you about this first day in Dubrovnik, the 28th of November, if I remember correctly. How did you know it then on that day, how did you dare touch something which perhaps was potentially explosive and dangerous? Is it possible that you touched some explosives without knowing what it was, what their properties were? How can you explain that? In fact, did you do that at all?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shrapnel on the wall was obviously quite dead. The cylinder that was in the rubble didn't have the head. Sir, I really take your point as a good point. This is the first time I had ever been near -- in a war zone. And one day when the Macedonian soldier was pulling the -- pulling the cylinder out of the wall and I was on the other side of the wall, and I was looking in the hole and putting my hand up the hole, I understood quickly that these things may seem to be dead but I wasn't sure that they were dead. It was an education for me, and I never behaved this way again in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just referred to a Macedonia soldier. Which Macedonian soldier are you talking about? How did you know -- how do you know that he was a Macedonian soldier? On whose side was he and on whose side was he fighting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to continue in the vein of your former question, sir, one day this gentleman -- actually, we were asking questions about shells and this gentleman very, very obligingly put a whole lot of live shells. They had been picked up around Dubrovnik in a little truck, and he drove it into the town, and he took these things out and showed them to us. We had an interpreter with us and explained that. Yes, I'm from Macedonia, I'm on the HVO -- sorry, wrong war. I'm in the Croatian defence forces, and this is the same gentleman I saw later pulling the tail out of the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an explosives expert or what was he?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There didn't seem to be many experts around on our side. His function seemed to have been a rather dirty job of piling up and recuperating all the various bits of ordnance which were around the district of Dubrovnik. Whether or not he was really talented -- he was trained for it, I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where was this? He took this from the vicinity of Dubrovnik to the institute where you looked at these things. Where was this? He took them to the institute on his van?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately he didn't take them into the institute. He only took them out of his van and showed them to us. And I took some pictures. They were live rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he collecting them?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that these rounds were -- these were collected outside of the Old Town. There was an artillery round as well, not a mortar, not a cylinder, so the so-called rocket, something else that we didn't -- we never saw in the town. And it was something he collected from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of a vehicle he used to transport them? Did you see the vehicle he used?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at night. It was some little -- it was like an Renault pickup truck or something like that. A little van, a camionette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was at night that we took these rounds to you for the purpose of your examining them, and that was in the Old Town, in the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Culture in the Old Town, if I understood you correct, or rather in front of the institute?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the institute, outside. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he transporting these shells at night? Why did you do the whole thing at night, if you know why?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he took unexploded mines and explosives into the Old City with all the potential dangers that entailed?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not seem a very wise thing to do and I didn't think it was a very wise thing to be done. And we had a very short meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did with the explosive shells then? Where did he take them to?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they went after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps convey to the city authorities of Dubrovnik your concern about potentially dangerous explosives being moved about the streets of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We didn't ask to see them again, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that there were such shells being kept in the cellars, in the basements, of the Old Town? Did you hear any stories to that effect?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any stories like that in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Dubrovnik, where was The Hague Convention flag hoisted? On what buildings was it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the Sponza Palace, the palace of the rectors, on the cathedral, on St. Blaise. Maybe there were one of two others. Maybe the Franciscan monastery. The thing is that apparently some of the flags had been raised on the Rupa, there was a flag raised on the Rupa, but the wind had actually blown it down. They didn't have very many flags, and this is one thing that they complained about. They didn't have many and they didn't seem to go about making more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see The Hague Convention flag on the imperial fortress on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the flag on the fortress; however, I saw the flag on a media report or some Western journalist had gone up the hill and had taken pictures of the soldiers up on the top of the hill. And it was a quick view of what looked like The Hague Convention flag on the fortress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this perhaps ITN footage that you saw prior to your departure for Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It might be ITN, yes. And it certainly was prior to going to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you saw: "I have seen a videotape from British television station ITN in which The Hague Convention emblem was flying alongside the Croatian flag on the imperial fortress of Mount Srdj." Did I -- have I quoted you correctly, I mean your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, what you state in your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ITN or CNN or whoever, I'm not sure about that. But the fact is I did see the flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the forces of the Croatian army were deployed on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this fact represent a gross misuse of The Hague Convention emblem?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents a very gross misuse of The Hague Convention symbol outside of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you raise this question with your hosts in Dubrovnik? Did you tell them that you had seen on this footage The Hague Convention flag on Srdj? Did you point out what potential dangers this could carry for the city of Dubrovnik itself, the fact, that is, that The Hague Convention flag was being abused in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just at this point in time wish to interject and state that whether or not there was a misuse or there wasn't a misuse of Hague Convention symbols, that's -- I would submit is a legal question which will be for the determination of the Court, which if it is, of course, a matter which is appropriate to be decided in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you raise the question of the use of the flag with your hosts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not raise the question of the use of this flag outside of the Old Town with anybody in the town, with the officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you concerned over this abuse? Were you afraid of the consequences of such an abuse of The Hague convention flag? Because the same flag was also erected on Srdj from which the army, the Croatian army, was operating as well as on the Old City from which, as you claimed, there were no operations, no fire by the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean I don't think that the Hague convention flag on Fort Srdj was going to protect Fort Srdj or the soldiers from anybody. And I do not understand what the linkage would be between the misuse of that flag on a clearly military object and the use of the flag inside of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the abuse of such a symbol punishable, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: That's -- I would object to. That is a purely legal question and I don't think that this witness is qualified to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that under some of The Hague Convention flags, just like it was done in Srdj, no fire was opened in the Old City of Dubrovnik as well, because the same people are in question, the same military unit is concerned, the same military unit on Srdj, and the same military unit in and around the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying that there were soldiers are hiding and using these buildings to shoot out of the town from. I just don't -- never saw any military posts in any of these buildings. I didn't see soldiers using these buildings. I don't think there's any similarity at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able at all to see whether somebody was actually doing this, because when there was alarms sounded, when it was night, when there were attacks you were not everywhere in the Old Town. On the 6th of December you were deep down in the cellar. Do you know what was happening from the facilities on which this flag was erected, just like it was on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you've said, sir, I was -- either I was in my bed at night when the police hour struck, of course, or else on the 6th of December I was in the Dominican monastery, so I didn't see what was going on in the Old Town at those moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are -- you do not believe that those who are abusing The Hague Convention flag in Srdj, could also be doing the same thing in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to interject. The witness has given his answer. Any further additional statement he can make it's -- that would be probably pure speculation, so I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness had decidedly said on several occasions that he hadn't seen anything of the kind, so I'm asking him whether he allows for the possibility that something of the kind might have happened when he was not looking, drawing a parallel when what had happened from Srdj, which was also flying The Hague Convention flag, like the city of Dubrovnik. I'm just asking him whether something like that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are, I would suggest, Mr. Petrovic, clearly reaching the point of conjecture there. The evidence, I think, of the witness is clear, which indicates that he saw footage of this flag being used on Mount Srdj. He has told you he saw no sign of an equivalent military abuse of the use of the flags in the city, the Old Town, but he has told you that there were times when he was indoors and did not see what was happening outdoors. He really can't take the matter any further, can he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept everything you have said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your knowledge, what is the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik? What was its role?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Crisis Staffs in the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the time of war were in fact groups of -- they were the officials of the town. Perhaps other people could be associated with them, and their role was simply that it was the management, the management of the affairs in the town in times of crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that the Crisis Staff was also in charge of defence matters in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know very much about the Crisis Staffs in general, and I don't know about the specific attributions of the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the seat of the Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone from the Crisis Staff? If so, where?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed that most of the municipal officials were on the Crisis Staff, and I met the mayor, and I met the deputy mayor, and I met one or two city councillors. Maybe -- I'm -- I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, where was it that you first carried out an on-site inspection of a building in Dubrovnik, which was in effect the first building that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first building was on Ulice Boskoviceva, and that would have been on the 28th, the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where specifically Boskoviceva Street is inside the Old Town? Can you remember its approximate location?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a few streets -- you're going westward, and it's a few streets down from the Sponza Palace. It's on the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the further course of our testimony, if I show you a map will you be able to pinpoint this exact spot on the map?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how good your map is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also referred to the fact that you had been to a woman's house on that first day which had been hit by several shells.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was her home inside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where specifically?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about Boskoviceva Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to that lady?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke to another lady, if I'm not mistaken, whose son had been killed while a member of the Croatian army - I'm not sure if I got this right - whose house had also been damaged.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are examples of people I spoke with, but it's -- they're far from exhaustive. I spoke with a great many people before the 6th of December, and afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that and we'll examine that in quite some detail, but what I want to know now is the following: This lady's house is near the dead bell, or Mrtvo Zvono, isn't that correct? And her son was killed where exactly, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was killed on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was her son a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly a member of the defence forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything interesting in the immediate surroundings of the house, something that you think would be noteworthy, something that needs to be mentioned before this Trial Chamber, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think I know to what you're alluding. You're alluding to what was clearly an observation post on St. Peter's Bastion. There were small works that had been added, I believe, by the Italians during the Italian occupation. And these provided shelter for one person. And there was a small post that was on St. Peter's Bastion; you could look out to the sea from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this inside the Old Town or, rather, on the walls?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the walls, and the walls are in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps observe that people were regularly standing guard there? Was there anything that could have led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people weren't really standing guard, but on the -- inside there was a little notebook which had times written on it. Now, I assume that -- because from that side I had seen a federal patrol boat. I assumed that this was the civil defence that was simply noting down the sightings of various patrol boats. I should say the patrol boats were very.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was not a place where someone was standing guard, then it must have been an observation post I assume?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an observation post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what do you think would have been the importance for the civilian protection to take down sightings of patrol boats? Or do you think maybe this was an offshore observation post used to observe the military observations that were underway in and around the town itself?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I assumed that this was simply for the boats. I cannot go any further than that. It's a very bad place to be observing anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information, do you think this would have been useful information to later be used by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments, for example?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't really get the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get you to explain what the importance of those data might have been. Could they have been used for civilian purposes, for cultural purposes, or was the only possible use when observing patrol boats passing by for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained what I saw, the notebook, the timings. I indicated that I had seen a patrol boat on one occasion. The third point is I know the people of Dubrovnik were very, very afraid of the patrol boats. And I can't speculate any further than that. I assumed it was for looking at patrol boats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice that observation was being conducted regularly from that position?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody in -- the only person I -- in that observation post was myself when I went to have a look and see what was inside of it. And I never saw anybody else inside of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This logbook, or notebook, that you referred to, what did it look like, the one that contained sightings? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was just a little notepad. It was lying there alone. Nobody walked off with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see regular entries in that logbook?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I looked at it once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see it or did you not see what I'm asking you about?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a certain number of timings that were noted down. I mean, I didn't interpret what those timings were or which days these were. I just saw these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that entries were -- had been made in different individual handwritings by different people, by people taking shifts obviously?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I can't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try to jog your memory on that, if I may. In your statement you say: "Just behind the house there was a small sentry point." That's what the B/C/S translation states. It may be a mistranslation, but that's at least how it was translated at the time. "I remember going in there and seeing a register of JRM ships sighted. I never saw anyone inside this facility, but it was clearly being regularly used, as there were entries on different dates and in different handwritings." Am I quoting you correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quoting me correctly, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true what the sentence says?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement is made three years ago. I will stand by the statement that I made three years ago. I've forgotten since.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the map that has been marked as P11. My apologies to the usher. P12 is the number, P12. [In English] This is too big. [Interpretation] My apologies. My apologies, Your Honours, I've selected the wrong map it seems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please just pull the map up a little bit so that we can see the southern portion of the town. The south, that's what we need. If you can just pull it up a little bit, please. Thank you. Just a little bit up, please. I can see it now, that's fine. Can you please point to the Mrtvo Zvono fort and why you said a while ago that you couldn't see anything from there when looking at the map this is the most prominent, outmost point of the town walls. What sort of a view over the surrounding sea is there from this point that you've just pointed out? Is it not the most prominent point of the whole Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's a very prominent point for observation over the sea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not natural that an observation post or a guard post should be there? Would not anyone who wanted to survey what was going on put an observation post there of all places? Can I please have an answer to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it there. There are also places you could put it on as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that this spot offers a wonderful view of the entire surrounding sea, on all sides around the town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll no longer be requiring this map. Thank you. Did you perhaps see any observation equipment being stored there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any observation equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see any communications equipment being kept there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that it was only on that spot that the town walls were being kept open all the time? Did you perhaps observe that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that strike you as strange, given the fact that the remaining portions of the walls were mostly kept closed?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't strike me as strange because there was precisely this little observation post there. So whoever would have access to it would want to have a fairly free access to it. So it's normal it would be kept open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform the town authorities of Dubrovnik that there was a guard post there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't inform them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that strike you as important? Did you think that it would have been important for you to notify the authorities?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- sir, as I assumed it was a civil defence, I assumed that the authorities would know that there was a post in existence. So there was no reason to inform them about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, sir, what is civilian protection and why would it be important for anyone referring to themselves as civilian protection to monitor movement of the JNA navy?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian protection would be an official body whose responsibility would be to make certain that things didn't happen to the people in the town or, just generally speaking, to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, why did it not occur to you that it was a military post and not a civilian post, perhaps? How come it first occurred to you that this was a civilian post? Why did it never occur to you that this might be a military post, a military place, a place used for military purposes? Why was not the first thing that occurred to you, but rather that it was a civilian post, given the fact that they were obviously monitoring ships and patrol boats?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not believe that there were soldiers carrying out the functions of soldiers in the Old Town. Secondly, as you have correctly pointed out, this is a superb observation post and it can be seen as well from everywhere. And it's a bit like, you know, soldiers in minarets and things like that. There's some very, very dangerous places, if you're going to be a soldier observing anything. So that's why I would call a reason far down the road. I assumed that the civil defence authorities had to have some sort of earlier warning system in the town so that they could just see that something was coming too close for comfort or there were too many of them and that they could give the alert right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This a priori refusal on your part that this could have been a military observation post, was this perhaps a result of the pressure exerted on you in the Old Town that no military should ever be observed, noticed in the Old Town, and no military installations?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. If I had seen that there were soldiers crawling over the St. Peter's Bastion, I certainly would have told somebody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would you have informed, had you seen soldiers around?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have gone to the mayor or to the vice-mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Poljanic and Mr. Obuljen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for example, if you had told them that you had seen soldiers around, they would have intervened and those soldiers would have been removed, I suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the way the question was phrased. The answer given previously was: If I had seen soldiers crawling all over St. Peter's Bastion I would have informed the mayor and the vice-mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will take a different approach now to clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any military, any soldiers, inside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on a number of occasions a few soldiers. Once I think I saw four or five -- five or six, something like that, and I said to Mr. Carnez, I've seen five or six soldiers. Do you know this is a cause for worry. You should talk to Mr. Obuljen. That was in the Old Town. Usually I would see one or two soldiers, and these soldiers were people who lived in the town and they were coming back from their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see those five or six soldiers in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't remember exactly. I think it was on the Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are sure that it was inside the Old Town, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know about these one or two soldiers that you had seen? How did you know that they lived inside the Old Town? Did you see them come in? Did you see what they were doing once inside the Old Town? How did you know that they resided in the Old Town? How come you knew that they were not on a mission since they were uniformed and carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were -- usually they weren't carrying weapons. I mean, on one or two occasions I saw people carrying long-barrelled weapons. But we talked to people and we said, What about these ones? They said, They live here. I didn't go up to them and question them about where they lived and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you to do that? Those people with long barrels, they reside in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember asking somebody specifically about the people with the long barrels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those six soldiers you saw, where were they headed for? How did they strike you? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were like all the other soldiers. They didn't seem -- they were walking around -- walking into the town. They weren't doing anything particularly. They weren't going anywhere. I just remember seeing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know they were going anywhere in particular if you don't even know where you saw them. You merely know that you did see them. How would you be in a position to know where those soldiers were headed or what their tasks were?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I think I saw them on the Stradun, and I have no particular detailed memories of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you do if you saw armed people on the Stradun or what did you do specifically in this situation when you saw six armed people carrying long weapons on the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Mr. Carnez and I said, Look, I saw a bunch of soldiers and you should go and speak to Obuljen about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you assist me, please, Dr. Kaiser. You've spoken of seeing one or two soldiers and you recall on one occasion seeing perhaps five or six. You've also said that on occasions, but not always, you saw soldiers carrying long-barrelled weapons. Were the five or six soldiers carrying long-barrelled weapons? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what they were carrying. If they were carrying -- if they were carrying side arms. I'm sorry, my memories are very, very vague about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Petrovic, it was something that was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you think it important to inform someone immediately about the fact that you had seen those five or six soldiers?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly if we started seeing a group of five or six soldiers and we started seeing more soldiers, we get really worried about the situation. It was important for us, as vague as my memories are, it was important for us to identify if something -- if there were people moving around and there were too many of them moving around. I mean, we could understand that one or two or three soldiers, maybe five soldiers, could be coming down from the mountain or coming from some other part of the -- you know, of their positions. But we would be very concerned if we started to see regularly large bunches of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what was it that worried you most about that? Why did you find that to be worrying?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think we were the only ones that could see eventually who was walking around in the town. They could be observed, I think, from outside the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no doubt about the fact that they could be observed in the Old Town as well as outside the Old Town. My question is: Why did that cause you concern?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This town was supposed to be as empty as possible of all military presence. Whether that be people in uniforms, whether that be whatever, this town was not supposed to have a military presence. So we had to keep our eyes open. We went around the walls in order to look at things, looking at clock towers, and church towers. Clamoured up in a few of them. We went around to see if there was anything on the walls, if there was any spent cartridge cases. Our mission was to make certain that the town was protected, and the best way to protect it was that there would not be military presence in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were there supposed to be no armed soldiers in the Old Town? What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were armed soldiers in a town, then somebody could say that these armed soldiers in the town are shooting at the federal forces outside of the town. We don't want -- we are trying to make certain that there could be no pretext, not pretext at all for any targeting on the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that was thinking about that when you were not on the Stradun, when you were in bed or perhaps sleeping, prior to the 28th of November? Who was it that worried about that? And who was there to prevent those people from doing the same thing as you saw them doing when you were there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not there to prevent them. This was something that the authorities of the town would have to make certain was respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient point, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. We may as well have a break now, yes. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaiser, please tell me, did you convey your concern about the armed soldiers in the Old Town to the Crisis Staff of the city?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion I mentioned I conveyed my concern to Mr. Carnez and then Mr. Carnez conveyed his concern to Mr. Obuljen, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you intervene the very first time that you saw soldiers in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only inter -- I only intervened about the question of this five or six soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the first meeting that you had with the Crisis Staff, did you accentuate how important it was for no military effectives of the Croatian side to be present in the city? Was that not one of the most important things that you said to them, given the importance of that question in the first encounter that you had immediately upon arrival with the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember what we conveyed to them the very first time because we had a general meeting, I think, in the mayor's office, and then we had a lunch, and I'm sorry I can't remember exactly what we conveyed. We explained generally our mission to them. You must remember that I was the cultural heritage consultant and I did not take care of contacts usually with the -- any of the city officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you said the following: "The staff in the mayor's office would be immediately informed by us when we saw more than two or three soldiers. We would inform Nikola Obuljen of this and we would take care that these soldiers left the Old City. We had to convey things of this kind to Obuljen on only a few occasions." Did I quote this part of your statement correctly? "There were very few occasions when we had cause to make such a report to Obuljen."

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please tell me as far as I can see here you speak in the plural, "we would, we had to, we had cause," and so on and so forth. Who were "we"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the observer mission. I am saying "we," but in fact Mr. Carnez had the -- he was the one who usually spoke to the members of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you yourself ever attended these talks?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend these talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you say here Mr. Carnez would intervene. Why did you say "we would intervene"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was intervening with Mr. Carnez; Mr. Carnez was intervening with the officials. I mean, I didn't intervene myself with the officials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then what would Mr. Carnez then say to the officials in the Crisis Staff? Would he then convey to them what you had seen? Would it be confined to that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would convey what we -- what I had seen or what he had seen, and that we didn't want to see soldiers. We wanted to see as few as possible soldiers in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did this on several occasions, as you speak in the plural here?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Carnez intervened on a number -- one or other -- one or more occasions. I remember mentioning once to Mr. Carnez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd report about this to Nikola Obuljen who on the Crisis Staff was in charge of military matters of the armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not certain exactly what Mr. Obuljen was in charge of on the Crisis Staff. He was an engineer I believe, and I thought he was mainly in charge of trying to keep some basic services working in the town. But I can't say for sure what all of his responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you made such reports, when you informed Mr. Obuljen about these things, would these soldiers then be removed from the town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the word "removed" is -- there would be fewer of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning that some of them would remain then. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't follow what individual soldiers were doing, going to see their families or coming back to stay for five days. This was not what my job was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it hence an effective way to reduce the number of soldiers that you saw to call Mr. Obuljen. And once Mr. Obuljen was called he would influence their number to be reduced. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about something that happened over a period of three weeks, which is to say that before the bombardment of the 6th of December and also in the two weeks after the bombardment of the 6th of December. I didn't write down anywhere any time I saw a soldier. I didn't write down a date when I saw a soldier. This is just something that happened from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I asked you was whether intervening with Obuljen was effective, whether it had an effect. I actually did not ask what you replied.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if we didn't see soldiers very often, then I could assume it also had an effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of a uniform Mr. Nikola Obuljen wore?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Obuljen didn't wear any uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this person, this man in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he is the commander of the -- he is one of the commanders of the armed forces of the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not know that he was one of the commanders of the armed forces in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that on the 7th of December he signed an agreement with the JNA forces on a cessation of hostilities, a ceasefire agreement, that is where he is designated as Mr. Obuljen, the commander of the armed forces of the city of Dubrovnik, and this is a document that was discussed before this Honourable Chamber by this gentleman who is fond of horses and dogs, whom you saw in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a little surprised, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you warned the authorities in Dubrovnik that uniformed men could not move around the Old City, do you think that they took some measures in order to evade your supervision and your warnings of this kind?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was any -- any evasion. But what kind of evasion are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps men who were members of the armed forces, did they perhaps carry out their combat mission in civilian clothes rather than in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I suppose that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to put a picture on the ELMO and also to present a copy to the Chamber and my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the limited resources that we have, I have been able only to reproduce one colour photograph. So I'll try to also make the other photographs. But for now, I've only been able to produce this one and I'll explain what this is. This is a photograph which was taken off the footage that the witness Ivo Grbic, whom you will certainly recall, who took the stand here and which he gave to my learned colleague, Mr. Weiner, which he disclosed to us. So this was a photograph which was taken off that video footage. Do you see this man, sir? Is he wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It indeed appears so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see this uniform or this kind of a uniform in the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- is that a uniform?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course it is not. These are civilian clothes. Can you see what this person, what this man on this photograph, is doing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appears to be loading a mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that he is loading a mortar and also opening mortar fire from a park which is some 200 metres under the city walls. That is, he is operating from Bogisicev Park in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be surprised now, because an investigator who took my statement back in 2001 pointed out that this activity was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice activities of this kind, that is to say people in Mufti opening mortar fire directly from the Old City and operating from inside the city?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you didn't see civilians opening fire from other positions either, not only from this part which is some 200 metres under the old city ramparts also in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When would I have seen this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On no occasion during your stay in the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned somebody near Dubrovnik opening fire on federal positions. I'm saying to you that I never had any occasion to see or to believe that such fire was being opened from near the city. I did not see or hear any such thing take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you say: "The investigator Stephens informed me that the investigation which was undertaken by the international Tribunal showed that the Croats had opened fire from the mortar position in Bogisicev Park several hundred metres away from the Old City." And then you say: "I was surprised because during this observation mission in Dubrovnik, I never saw anything which would indicate that Croats were operating from such weapons so near the Old Town." Did I quote your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I have your leave for this photograph to be marked as evidence, and I shall do my best to also prepare colour photographs -- copies for you and for the other side. But we are -- our resources are limited and that poses quite a problem for us. So this is - let me repeat - footage which was identified and handed over to the Prosecution by the witness Grbic who took the stand before the Honourable Chamber a few weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
